body: Friday, July 17 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed under Chair Warsh remains hawkish in rhetoric — "prices are too high" — while markets have shifted from expecting cuts to pricing in possible hike risk at the July meeting. The 10Y yield at 4.55 (+9 bps vs 4W) and 2Y at 4.16 (prior close, +11 bps vs 4W) confirm a rising-rate environment. The curve is positively sloped at +41 bps — still flat by historical standards — reflecting term premium repricing rather than inversion-driven recession fear. Consumer sentiment beat expectations this week, but building permits declined more than forecast, revealing a bifurcated economy.

New / Most Important: The structural story this week is the Great Rotation away from megacap tech. Nasdaq 100 is down 2.8% vs 4W while Russell 2000 is up 1.7% — the Russell/Nasdaq ratio surged 4.6% over 4 weeks, its most decisive breadth expansion in this cycle. CNBC reported rising odds of a July Fed rate hike, which — if it materializes — would be the first hike in this phase of the cycle and a genuine regime break. June CPI showed a slowdown that "weakened hike expectations" per Korean press, but the Iran-driven energy supply shock is keeping the Fed boxed. This is a fundamentally new policy trap: a Fed Chair who wants to signal hawkishness on inflation but faces a labor market that is stable and an economy tracking near Q1 pace. The hike talk may be jawboning to keep financial conditions tight without acting, but the market is taking it seriously enough to push 2Y yields higher. BofA calling for a strong dollar second half aligns with this hawkish hold posture.

Playbook ✓: Rising oil prices from Middle East escalation feeding through to sticky inflation expectations, keeping the Fed on hold — textbook supply-shock bind.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The divergence is the VIX at 17.86 (↓3.1% vs 4W) sitting in COMPLACENCY territory while hike risk builds and tech sells off hard. Equity vol is not pricing the tail risk of a Fed that actually hikes into a semiconductor-led growth scare. Gold is down 7.8% vs 4W despite a hot geopolitical backdrop — this is NOT the fear-bid playbook; it suggests real rates are rising fast enough to overwhelm safe-haven demand. BTC up 6.6% vs 4W while gold craters (divergence of -14.3pp) signals the market is treating crypto as a risk-on liquidity proxy, not a macro hedge. This combination — rising yields, falling gold, falling vol, rotating equities — is consistent with a "tightening that works" regime where liquidity drains from duration-sensitive assets into value/cyclicals, but it could snap violently if the hike actually happens.

Macro Stance: The ECB is expected to hold rates at its July 23 meeting per Morningstar, but the September hike probability is rising on renewed Strait of Hormuz energy price pressures. Eurozone bond yields are climbing as oil-driven inflation complicates the easing narrative the ECB held through early 2026. Bank of Italy flagged slower Q2 growth, underscoring the stagflationary bind.

New / Most Important: The ECB's pivot from a tentative easing bias toward "tightening hopes" (per FXStreet) is structurally significant. Hormuz hostilities have forced a complete rates rethink — CNBC described the outlook as "extremely volatile." This is the eurozone's chronic vulnerability: an energy-importing bloc where supply-shock inflation directly competes with weak domestic demand. The digital euro pilot advancing with 36 providers is notable for medium-term plumbing but not market-moving today. The UK economy tracking "materially stronger than expected" creates further intra-European divergence that complicates a unified ECB stance.

Playbook ✓: Energy price pass-through forcing hawkish ECB hold — exactly the supply-shock playbook.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The divergence is that euro is "steadying" rather than weakening against majors despite a growth downgrade from Italy and rising oil import costs. This suggests the market is pricing ECB hawkishness as credible, or alternatively that dollar weakness from U.S. fiscal concerns is offsetting eurozone fundamentals. Watch HICP data — if core inflation re-accelerates, the September hike becomes consensus rather than tail risk.

Macro Stance: The PBOC is managing, not cutting. It sees a stable renminbi amid two-way fluctuations (China Daily, [Jul 16]), is moving to deepen offshore yuan liquidity and broaden asset supply (Caixin, [Jul 16]), and flagged slower credit growth as a "new normal" (Caixin, [Jul 16]). Front-end support came through tax-week liquidity (Bloomberg, [Jul 14]) with a floor that bills not be re-discounted below 0.5% (Reuters, [Jul 14]). Prices: June CPI rose 1% (Global Times, [Jul 9]) and producer inflation hit a four-year high (Reuters, [Jul 8]), which Bloomberg calls "bad inflation" ([Jul 15]).

PMIs & Activity: Second-quarter GDP grew 4.3%, below the official target range (Bloomberg, [Jul 15]), even as June industrial output rose 5.3% y/y and retail sales returned to growth (BusinessLine, [Jul 15]) and the urban unemployment rate fell further (China Daily, [Jul 16]). The engine is narrow: Capital Economics says AI is now the main driver of growth ([Jul 16]) and the WSJ describes a two-speed economy pairing high-tech success with domestic gloom ([Jul 16]). Investment is sliding as infrastructure joins property (Caixin, [Jul 15]), exports jumped 27% y/y in June (Reuters, [Jul 13]) and the official manufacturing PMI was 50.3 (Reuters, [Jun 29]). July has started soft, with NEV retail sales down 8% in the first two weeks (CnEVPost, [Jul 15]).

Credit Impulse: June credit growth missed forecasts (Caixin, [Jul 16]) and new bank loans rose less than expected (The Star, [Jul 15]). In May the headline beat because government bonds carried total social financing to 7.7% growth (CGTN, [Jun 12]) while loans missed (Reuters, [Jun 12]); in June neither leg delivered. Record consumer defaults undermine the push to boost spending (Reuters, [Jul 15]), LGFVs that have added debt face curbs on new bonds (Bloomberg, [Jul 15]), and one of China's top investors says finance, not AI, is the country's biggest bottleneck (CNBC, [Jul 16]). With the PBOC calling slower credit the new normal, the impulse is flat at best.

Property: Property investment slumped 18% y/y in January–June (The Standard, [Jul 15]). Prices are stabilising only at the top: first-tier home prices extended a four-month rebound (SCMP, [Jul 15]), while nationally new home prices declined at a slower pace (The Standard, [Jul 15]). Developers face a fresh liquidity crunch (Nikkei Asia, [Jul 13]), and Morgan Stanley is screening for property stocks that can weather near-term weakness (Investing.com, [Jul 16]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Beijing is betting on faster state-backed projects to shore up growth and avoid broad stimulus (Reuters, [Jul 16]), while Breakingviews warns the local-debt cleanup leaves a growth mess (Reuters, [Jul 16]) and Westpac argues for urgent stimulus ([Jul 15]). The July Politburo meeting is being prepared (Sinocism, [Jul 13]). Europe is hardening: Merz is inching Germany toward backing an EU push against China (Bloomberg, [Jul 16]), and Brussels is preparing an emergency response to renewed rare-earth controls (EU Today, [Jul 16]) after the IEA put $6.5 trillion of Western industry at risk (Reuters, [Jul 15]). With Washington the mood is calmer: the first US LNG cargo in a year docked in China (Bloomberg, [Jul 16]).

Markets & Flows: The AI trade cracked on the mainland. ChiNext plunged over 7% as nearly 5,000 stocks fell in the global tech sell-off (BigGo Finance, [Jul 16]), the Shanghai benchmark lost 1.85% on weak GDP data and the chip sell-off (BBN Times, [Jul 16]), and the chip pullback drove investor fear to a record high (Bloomberg, [Jul 16]). CXMT's $8.6 billion IPO drew less frenzied demand (Reuters, [Jul 16]). Hong Kong diverged, reclaiming 25,000 (Moomoo, [Jul 16]) as Alibaba jumped 7.9% on the Apple AI approval (TradingView, [Jul 16]), though its discount to China widened on liquidity pressure (Bloomberg, [Jul 16]).

New / Most Important: Beijing has chosen its response to the growth miss: faster state-backed projects, not broad stimulus, alongside a central bank that calls slower credit the new normal. That puts the burden on the state balance sheet just as the local-debt cleanup constrains it, and leaves the private side, where loans missed and defaults are at a record, without a direct lift. The ChiNext rout matters for the same reason: if the AI engine that carried the quarter wobbles, there is no domestic-demand engine ready to take over before the Politburo meets.

Playbook ✓: Targeted, investment-led support, a managed yuan, weak private credit and a property drag are on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The consensus wanted a demand stimulus after a 4.3% quarter; Beijing is offering projects and a stable currency instead. The transmission splits by asset. Faster state-backed projects are a modest positive for bulk demand, and BHP has already won higher quarterly iron ore prices despite China's buying curbs (Reuters, [Jul 16]), a near-term support for AUD that property investment down 18% will limit. European exporters face the opposite: no Chinese demand push, a record surplus and a German government drifting toward EU action. Oil gains nothing from a project-led plan while Chinese crude imports sit near a decade low, and EM Asia's AI-hardware exporters now carry China's chip-sector volatility.

Macro Stance: Japan is caught in a three-way policy collision: the BOJ signaling further hikes, the Takaichi government pushing back, and the yen at multi-decade lows triggering intervention risk. USD/JPY above 160 per the feed, with forecasters eyeing 175 — this is a structural crisis, not a cyclical one.

New / Most Important: This week's most important development is the BOJ bond-buying pause, which left the yen further exposed to depreciation and raised intervention risk. The contradiction between BOJ hawkishness and government resistance is now openly rattling both bond and currency markets — JAPAN Forward described the signals as "contradictory." The weak yen is described as a "structural crisis" by ThinkChina, not merely a cyclical adjustment. This is a new regime: Japan has moved from deflation-era ZIRP to a world where it needs to hike rates to defend the currency, but hiking rates threatens the government's fiscal position given the world's highest debt-to-GDP ratio. The bond-buying pause is the BOJ trying to let JGB yields rise without actively selling — a passive tightening that risks losing control of both ends. If USD/JPY breaches 175, intervention alone won't stabilize the currency; the BOJ would need a credible, sustained tightening cycle. Many Japanese firms now cite weak yen as a bigger worry than BOJ rate hikes, signaling that corporate Japan has flipped from yen-weakness beneficiary to victim.

Playbook ✓: BOJ gradually normalizing policy while managing curve — standard exit playbook.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The divergence is that the BOJ pause in bond buying is failing to stabilize the yen — the market is calling the bluff on gradual normalization and demanding faster action. EUR/JPY in the upper 185 range with Iran tensions capping gains suggests the yen is losing its safe-haven bid even in a geopolitical risk environment.

Macro Stance: Australia faces a potential fourth rate hike in this cycle, with Westpac and a major bank (Sky News) both signaling imminent action. The Iran-driven energy price shock is the proximate trigger — The Guardian reported a hike becomes more likely if the Iran conflict isn't resolved within a week. Rate cut expectations have been pushed out to 2027.

New / Most Important: This is a structurally important shift. Australia was supposed to be pivoting to cuts by now; instead, the RBA is being forced into a procyclical hike by an exogenous supply shock, against the backdrop of a Chinese investment slump — property investment fell 18% y/y in January–June and infrastructure has joined the decline — that threatens demand for Australia's bulk exports, even though BHP has so far won higher quarterly iron ore prices. The terms-of-trade squeeze — rising energy import costs against softening Chinese construction demand — is a classic emerging-market dynamic hitting a developed economy. Brokers and lenders are placing bets on the next move, and the consensus has shifted firmly hawkish. The political angle (Joyce's criticism of the RBA, the "contingency plan misrepresented as recession warning") signals growing friction between the government and the central bank.

Playbook ✓: Energy-driven inflation forcing hawkish posture — standard.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Hiking into a China-led construction downturn is the divergence. Australia's macro model depends on Chinese demand; with China's second-quarter growth at 4.3%, below target, and June new loans missing forecasts, that leg is weakening precisely as the RBA tightens. This risks a policy error where the RBA fights supply-side inflation by crushing demand-side growth.

Macro Stance: The week ends with the NBP's hawks setting the tone. The bank disclosed which members voted for a hike at an earlier meeting (Tysol.pl, [Jul 17]), a Council member repeated that increases are more probable than cuts (Radio ESKA, [Jul 17]; Business Insider Polska, [Jul 16]), and Direct Money warns mortgage holders the forecast may mean higher instalments for many months ([Jul 17]). That is a long way from the governor's offer, only a week old, to file a cut motion after the holidays (Polskie Radio 24, [Jul 10]). Rates are unchanged after the July hold (CEO Magazyn, [Jul 10]) and Erste still sees no cuts before end-2027 (Direct Money, [Jul 10]). The data give both camps ammunition: June CPI was confirmed at 2.5% y/y with prices down 0.5% m/m (Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK, [Jul 15]) and core inflation fell (Biznes Wprost, [Jul 16]), but Eurostat's HICP measure puts Polish inflation at 3% y/y in June (Do Rzeczy, [Jul 17]), prices are rising faster than the EU average (Business Insider Polska, [Jul 17]), and the CPN fuel package has expired, which Gazeta Prawna and Erste expect to lift July inflation ([Jul 15]) while PKO BP sees a transitory move above 3.5% (PAP, [Jul 15]). The oil connection is explicit: the finance minister has "no good news" on pump prices (Business Insider Polska, [Jul 17]) and does not rule out bringing CPN back (Interia Motoryzacja, FXMAG, [Jul 17]).

Markets: Friday was risk-off: "copper and geopolitics sank KGHM and the banks", Orlen and Żabka stayed green, and Rzeczpospolita saw investors "fleeing before the weekend" (Parkiet, Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 17]). Żabka rose a further 10.87% on reports that Seven & i is in advanced talks over a multibillion-dollar stake (FXMAG, Yahoo Finance, Inside Retail Asia, [Jul 17]), while KGHM lost 3.32% (FXMAG, [Jul 17]). Bankier's Masłowski calls this "an advanced phase of the bull market", with Allegro, Pepco and Żabka no longer cheap and at their most expensive in years ([Jul 17]), and Parkiet notes the WIG20 laggards that never joined the rally are leaving investors counting losses ([Jul 17]). The card before Friday's session: Allegro 44.37 (+13.9% 1W, +15.3% 4W), Orlen 145.88 (+4.6% / +16.6%), LPP 20040 (+6.6% / +6.9%), Dino 29.43 (+6.1% / +1.1%), CD Projekt 234.6 (+1.3% / +5.2%), PGE 9.28 (-0.3% / -4.9%), KGHM 303.0 (-0.5% / -19.0%), PKO 107.98 (+0.3% / +2.4%) and Pekao 233.3 (-0.9% / -1.0%); EPOL 40.64 is +2.7% 1W but -0.1% 4W. StockWatch counts five blue chips still due to pay 13.7 billion zloty of dividends this season ([Jul 17]). The zloty broke down: EUR/PLN tested 4.35, the highest for the euro since November 2024, and FXMAG reports "the zloty and Polish bonds strongly down" with EUR/PLN back above 4.33 and EUR/USD at 1.1440 (Interia Biznes, Business Insider Polska, FXMAG, TVN24, [Jul 17]). The card has USD/PLN 3.7782 (-0.2% 1W, +1.8% 4W) and EUR/PLN 4.328 (0.0% / +1.7%). The week's POLGB auction had already disappointed (wnp.pl, [Jul 16]).

Fiscal & Politics: Domański put numbers on the cost of presidential vetoes and said they "weaken the whole potential of the economy" (TVN24, Wiadomości Onet, [Jul 17]), while GlobEnergia prices the CPN package at 4.7 billion zloty for 92 days of relief, deepening a deficit of 123.7 billion zloty after June (GlobEnergia, [Jul 17]; Gazeta Prawna, [Jul 16]). Public debt stands at 2.5 trillion zloty (wPolityce.pl, [Jul 14]), German media rate the economy as strong growth with a weak point in rising debt (Interia Biznes, Money.pl, [Jul 17]), and Bulgaria's post-euro deficit procedure is the cautionary tale (Obserwator Gospodarczy, [Jul 17]). Tax changes for 2027 are settled with new rates (wnp.pl, [Jul 17]) and Domański left the door ajar to a higher PIT threshold (Fakt, [Jul 17]). The Sejm rejected the president's bill to cut VAT on electricity (Bankier.pl, [Jul 17]) and the KAS audits' 120 billion zloty of irregularities are now with prosecutors (Polskie Radio 24, [Jul 17]).

Corporate & Sectors: The bank sector took two hits: President Nawrocki signed the CHF law, which speeds court handling and lets borrowers suspend repayments once they sue (Bankier.pl, Next Gazeta.pl, Radio ESKA, [Jul 17]), the Supreme Court sided with CHF borrowers (Super Biznes, [Jul 17]), and the NBP's warning of a new wave of lawsuits (Parkiet, [Jul 14]) sits alongside the proposed CIT increase (pb.pl, [Jul 14]). Also, PKO BP will switch off services and mobile authorisation for scheduled maintenance this weekend (Polskie Radio 24, GSMonline, [Jul 17]). The Sejm passed the Water Law amendment Orlen Termika lobbied for (wnp.pl, [Jul 17]), and Żerań's heat accumulator, Europe's largest, is largely complete (PAP, [Jul 16]). Dino's lawsuit against a union leader has become a scandal (INNPoland.pl, [Jul 17]). The EU published its ETS reform and electrification plan (Gramwzielone.pl, [Jul 17]).

Geopolitics & Security: Türkiye Today frames Poland's "deepest fear" as a Russian test of NATO in the coming months ([Jul 17]), after a week of Polish and Baltic warnings of a limited military or hybrid provocation (AP News, [Jul 15]). Washington detailed new sanctions on Russia (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 17]). Domestic support for helping Ukraine has fallen from 77% to 52% (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 16]).

New / Most Important: The zloty's break to a post-2024 low against the euro while bonds sold off is the week's verdict on Poland's policy mix: a 123.7 billion zloty half-year deficit, a central bank whose public voices now talk hikes, and a CHF law that raises bank litigation risk. Equity has escaped so far on Allegro, Orlen and the Żabka bid, but Friday's bank and KGHM selling shows the index is not immune to the same oil-and-fiscal pressure the currency is pricing.

Playbook ✓: CEE central banks leading rate-cycle turns is the pattern; a currency selling off on fiscal slippage plus an oil shock is orthodox.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The NBP is being pushed toward holding or hiking while oil prices surge (WTI up 6.1% over four weeks) and the government debates re-subsidising fuel, which would widen the deficit that is weakening the zloty in the first place. Banks at records a week ago now carry CIT, CHF and rate-path risk simultaneously; the strategic bid for Żabka says foreign buyers prefer Polish consumers to Polish balance sheets.

Macro Stance: India's biggest IPO of 2026 drew $31 billion in bids, powered by institutional frenzy — a signal of massive domestic and foreign capital allocation into Indian equities. This is a structural flow story: as global capital rotates out of megacap tech, India's growth premium and deep domestic savings pool are attracting outsized interest.

New / Most Important: The $31B bid-to-cover on a single IPO is a capital-flow event, not just a stock story. It signals that India is absorbing liquidity that might otherwise chase U.S. tech or China. The Russell/Nasdaq rotation in the U.S. has a global parallel: money is flowing from concentrated mega-cap bets to broader, higher-growth stories. India is the EM beneficiary.  |  Playbook ✓: India as China-alternative EM allocation — well-established thesis playing out.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The risk is oil. India is a net energy importer, and WTI at 81.45 (↑6.1% vs 4W) with Iran escalation ongoing threatens the current account and forces the RBI into a tighter stance. Institutional frenzy at cycle highs in an oil-vulnerable economy bears watching.

Narrative: The great tech unwind is underway: the Nasdaq 100 is down 2.8% vs 4W while the S&P 500 is up 1.0%, and the chip sell-off and fading faith in the AI chip trade are converging into "The Great Rotation" out of mega-cap tech.

Reported: Wipro lagged peers after an earnings miss and a weak forecast (Reuters, [Jul 16]), and Tech Mahindra's profit rose 28.4% but missed estimates (Business Standard, [Jul 16]). IBM plunged 25% after a second-quarter warning, its CEO admitting the company fell behind (Fortune, [Jul 15]).

EPS Upside Watch: Synopsys — raised its guidance, and JPMorgan says it is still too conservative (TIKR.com, [Jul 16]). Cloudflare — analysts are raising AI and security targets (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 16]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus held that AI capex would sustain tech multiples; the market is now learning that capex can be massive and margins compress at the same time. For most companies AI spending is a cost centre before it is a revenue line, and patience for that lag is fading as rates rise.
Narrative: Netflix's miss and underwhelming forecast dragged the sector, and Meta's AI pivot is being reframed from growth catalyst to capex burden.

Reported: Netflix's revenue fell short of estimates (Investing.com, [Jul 16]), and the stock fell as its forecast disappointed and it said it will give fewer engagement updates (CNBC, [Jul 16]). Publicis raised its guidance on new business wins (WSJ, [Jul 16]), while Telenor cut guidance for the second time in two quarters (Telecoms, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Alphabet — BofA Securities raised its target on cloud growth (Investing.com, [Jul 16]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Meta surged 13% as the AI capex story flips (Money Morning, [Jul 16]), and its reported $10B compute lease with Anthropic points to a new model: if hyperscalers become compute landlords, capex turns into rent, and the sector's bear case shifts from AI spenders to pure content plays like Netflix.

Narrative: Rising yields (10Y at 4.55, 2Y at 4.16) and a positively sloped but still-flat +41 bps curve are a modestly supportive NIM backdrop, and the rotation from tech into value and cyclicals benefits financials directly.

Reported: U.S. Bancorp posted record quarterly revenue on loan growth (Reuters, [Jul 16]), and State Street's profit jumped 56% on strong fee income (Reuters, [Jul 16]). Morgan Stanley posted record revenue and profit as equities trading surged 69% (CNBC, [Jul 15]), and BlackRock rallied 7% after its beat (TIKR.com, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Bank of America — its earnings were great, but the new guidance is the real story (Trefis, [Jul 16]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Deutsche Bank is flagged as exposed to inflation and geopolitical risk, making European banks the stress test of whether higher rates help when the cause is supply-shock inflation rather than demand-led growth.
Narrative: WTI at 81.45 (↑6.1% vs 4W) is pricing a supply shock from the US-Iran strikes, not demand pull: China's second-quarter GDP slowed to 4.3% and its crude imports sit near a decade low.

Reported: TotalEnergies expects higher second-quarter profit on the war-related price rally (Reuters, [Jul 16]), though its shares fell on a softer LNG outlook (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 16]). BP expects stronger quarterly earnings despite lower output (Kalkine Media, [Jul 14]) as oil trading results are poised to grow (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 14]).

EPS Upside Watch: European majors — European earnings growth is seen at its strongest in 3 years as energy profits surge (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 16]). Devon Energy — earnings expectations upgraded on estimate revisions (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 10]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Supply-shock rallies are supposed to destroy demand and self-correct, but AI data-centre power demand is building a structural floor under energy. Energy is both the inflation problem and the AI infrastructure solution, a duality the consensus underprices.

Narrative: Transportation stocks are fuelling the rally, Mexico's heavy-duty truck production and exports to the US rebounded in June as nearshoring capex turns real, and the Russell 2000 (↑1.7% vs 4W) carries the small-cap industrial bid.

Reported: GE Aerospace beat and lifted guidance on services growth (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 16]), but a near-perfect report wasn't enough for the stock (Barron's, [Jul 16]). ABB beat Q2 forecasts and announced a $5.5B Rotork acquisition (Global Banking & Finance Review, [Jul 16]). United beat and raised (Quartz, [Jul 15]), but its shares fell on a weak outlook (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Cintas — analysts are raising forecasts after an upbeat Q4 (Benzinga, [Jul 16]). Caterpillar — JPMorgan and Wells Fargo just raised their targets (TIKR.com, [Jul 15]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Building permits fell more than expected: industrials rally on transport and defence capex while the residential pipeline weakens under rising rates, a split inside XLI that could widen.
Narrative: Consumer sentiment beat expectations, but rising energy costs create cross-currents, and Tesla still draws retail attention while institutional positioning stays cautious.

Reported: Frasers Group grew revenue and retail profits as international expansion accelerates (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 16]). Richemont's sales beat lifted the luxury sector as jewellery shines (Reuters, [Jul 15]). Rank Group raised profit guidance on digital growth and gaming machines (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 14]).
EPS Upside Watch: Amazon — Wall Street is raising its target ahead of earnings (Watcher Guru, [Jul 16]). Tesla — four price-target hikes ahead of Q2 earnings (Investor's Business Daily, [Jul 14]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Sentiment beating while building permits fall is the classic late-cycle divergence: consumers feel fine on asset prices while real activity slows. Worth monitoring, not yet actionable.
Narrative: Staples benefit from defensive rotation in a tech-led sell-off, but rising input costs from oil and supply-chain disruption limit margin expansion.

Reported: Conagra fell as guidance disappointed and it cut its dividend (Barron's, [Jul 15]), alongside a $2 billion charge (MarketWatch, [Jul 15]). Heritage Foods' net profit plunged 38% as margins shrank (NDTV Profit, [Jul 16]). PepsiCo's turnaround stutters as Americans rethink snacking (ET BrandEquity, [Jul 15]).
EPS Upside Watch: Walmart — another move to win higher-income shoppers (TheStreet, [Jul 14]) supports mix and margins.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The defensive bid is not reaching packaged food: after Conagra's cut, Barron's lists 6 more food stock payouts at risk (Barron's, [Jul 15]). Volumes, not just input costs, are the binding constraint.
Narrative: Healthcare benefits from the rotation into defensives, but results are being judged stock by stock rather than as a sector bid.

Reported: UnitedHealth blew past estimates and hiked its earnings outlook as it reins in costs (CNBC, [Jul 16]). Abbott raised its 2026 profit forecast on strength in diagnostics and medical devices (Reuters, [Jul 16]). Intuitive Surgical beat Q2 estimates, but the shares fell (Investing.com, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Humana — earnings estimates are rising (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 16]) as managed-care cost trends improve.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Medtech beats are being sold while managed care, the recent laggard, rallies on cost control: J&J posted a solid quarter yet Wall Street sold off (NAI500, [Jul 16]). The rotation is happening inside healthcare, not only into it.

Narrative: Copper at 6.26 (↓3.3% vs 4W) trades as an AI data-centre and grid-capex metal and is sliding with the semiconductor rout, while gold, down 7.8%, is crushed by rising real yields. The cyclical read comes from China: property investment fell 18% y/y in January–June and Beijing leans on faster state-backed projects rather than broad stimulus.

Reported: Alcoa cut production guidance (WSJ, [Jul 16]), and the shares tumbled after a cyclone cut alumina output (Mining.com, [Jul 16]). BASF lifted guidance as higher chemical prices boost earnings (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 15]). Himadri Speciality hit a 52-week high as profit soared 27% (Upstox, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold falling sharply during an active US-Iran military conflict breaks the geopolitical-hedge playbook: the real-rate surge from hawkish Fed and ECB postures is dominating, the strongest sign that the global liquidity cycle has turned tighter.
Narrative: Building permits declined more than expected while yields rise, the worst combination for rate-sensitive REITs, and there is no rate relief in sight with the Fed leaning hawkish.

Reported: Prologis raised guidance after a record quarter for leasing (Estates Gazette, [Jul 16]). UK housebuilder Crest Nicholson sank to a loss amid a 'challenging' housing market (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Data-centre REITs — AI compute demand is the structural floor, though rising power costs from the energy shock bite.
